newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds calls expert on 'common knowledge'.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds calls expert on 'common knowledge'.

text.p: Lawyers for R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co called a historian to the witness stand Monday at a wrongful death trial to testify on the issue of "common knowledge" about cigarette smoking.

Over the objections of lawyers for plaintiff Dana Raulerson, Judge Bernard Nachman said he would allow University of South Carolina history professor Lacy Ford to testify about what most people knew about cigarette smoking and when they knew it.

Raulerson sued the tobacco company for wrongful death on behalf of the estate and children of her late sister, Jean Connor, who smoked heavily for more than 30 years and died of lung cancer in October 1995.

Reynolds' lawyers said Ford was being called to talk about consumer expectations and knowledge, and the adequacy of notices related to the company's duty to warn the public about the risks of cigarette smoking.
Ron Motley, an attorney for Raulerson, objected on the grounds that Ford was not "capable of expert opinion, and how can someone opine what common knowledge was?"

Ford said he had studied national newspapers and magazines including the New York Times, Reader's Digest and Life, and local newspapers including the Florida Times-Union and Jacksonville Journal, to determine what was common knowledge about cigarette smoking from the turn of the century to 1969.

He said he also looked at public school curricula, including that of Duval County public schools, where Connor was educated, but did not examine medical journals or internal tobacco industry documents.
He defined common knowledge as "communal knowledge ... not what any individual has read from any source. It's broadly known."
He said common knowledge could be passed from generation to generation and was not necessarily true.
Defense lawyers appeared to be aiming to bolster their contention that Jean Connor chose to smoke despite the knowledge that smoking was a risk factor for disease.
Nachman said he would allow the testimony, noting that common knowledge would not be what Connor knew, but only what someone could reasonably have been expected to know.
He told lawyers for both sides to draw up suggested cautionary statements to be given to the jury on Tuesday morning before Ford's testimony, explaining how they could interpret "common knowledge."
Reynolds is a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
